prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Snowflake Inc." (ticker SNOW), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "SNOW", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Snowflake Inc.
result.industry: Cloud data and AI platform software
markets: Enterprise AI and AI agents on company data

mission.statement: to empower every enterprise to achieve its full potential through data and AI
mission.plain: Help every company get the most out of its data and AI.

about.plain: Snowflake runs a giant online place where companies keep all their information, like sales, customers and stock levels. Workers can ask questions of that information and get answers fast, without owning their own computers to do it. Its AI tools let people ask in plain words and let AI helpers do work using the company's data. Companies pay for how much computing they use, a bit like an electricity bill.
about.customers: Mostly large and mid-sized companies, including 829 of the world's 2,000 biggest companies, plus government agencies.
about.everyday: When a bank, retailer or streaming service studies what millions of customers do, that number-crunching often runs on Snowflake.

money.plain: pay-as-you-go computing and storage to store, process and analyse data
experts who help customers set up and move data
CoWork (formerly Snowflake Intelligence) and Cortex Code AI helpers that work on company data
managed everyday databases that run apps, from the 2025 Crunchy Data deal
tools that watch software systems for problems, from the February 2026 Observe acquisition

result.summary: Snowflake has a real but contested advantage: data and workloads are sticky once loaded (net revenue retention of 126% in Q2 FY2027, 828 customers spending over $1 million a year) and its data-sharing network gets more useful as more companies join. But Databricks and the big cloud providers (AWS, Microsoft, Google) offer strong substitutes, open table formats like Apache Iceberg make data easier to move, and its consumption pricing means customers can cut usage quickly, so the moat is moderate rather than dominant.

pricingPower.evidence: Snowflake charges per credit consumed and has not relied on list-price rises; its performance improvements lower customer bills, and FY2027 guidance lowers non-GAAP product gross margin to 74% from 76% in FY2026 as AI compute costs rise, yet product revenue growth accelerated to 37% in Q2 FY2027 with 126% net revenue retention.

moats.evidence: Snowflake is a well-known enterprise data brand used by 829 Forbes Global 2000 companies, but it is little known to consumers and the brand does not command a price premium on its own.

Customers build data pipelines, governance, dashboards and apps on Snowflake, shown by 126% net revenue retention and $9.00 billion of remaining performance obligations at July 31, 2026; Iceberg support makes the data itself more portable over time.

Snowflake Marketplace and secure data sharing let companies share live data with suppliers and partners without copying it, so each new customer makes the network more valuable to others in industries like financial services and advertising.
Snowflake rents its infrastructure from AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, who are also competitors, so it has no structural cost edge; its 67% GAAP gross margin is below many software peers.
The cloud data market supports many large players (Databricks, AWS, Microsoft, Google, Oracle), so there is no natural limit on competitors.
Its multi-cloud, cloud-neutral position lets customers run across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, which a hyperscaler pushing its own cloud cannot easily copy.
Its separated storage-and-compute architecture, built by co-founders from Oracle's database team since 2012, gives an easy, near-zero-maintenance service that rivals have taken years to match.
It has strong database talent and partnerships (such as its $200 million OpenAI deal), but no exclusive asset that rivals cannot obtain.

customers.evidence: Net revenue retention was 126% in Q2 FY2027, total customers reached 14,554 (up 32%), customers with over $1 million in trailing product revenue rose 27% to 828, and 65 customers spend over $10 million a year.

talent.evidence: Snowflake had 9,060 employees at January 31, 2026 and paid $1.71 billion of stock-based compensation in FY2026 (about $189,000 per employee), which helps attract engineers, though it is not a regular fixture at the top of public employer rankings.

product.evidence: Its fully managed, easy-to-use data platform is widely regarded as a leader in cloud data warehousing, and newer AI products are gaining fast: CoWork (formerly Snowflake Intelligence) and Cortex Code had thousands of customer accounts each by Q2 FY2027; Databricks remains an equally strong rival, especially for data science and AI.

competitors.name: Databricks
competitors.note: Private data and AI platform (lakehouse, Lakebase, Genie); the most direct rival, with a revenue run-rate above $7 billion in August 2026.

competitors.name: Microsoft
competitors.note: Microsoft Fabric, Azure Synapse and Azure SQL compete for analytics and data workloads (also a Snowflake partner).

competitors.name: Amazon (AWS)
competitors.note: Amazon Redshift, S3 data lakes and Athena compete, though AWS is also Snowflake's largest infrastructure partner and sales channel.

competitors.name: Alphabet (Google Cloud)
competitors.note: Google BigQuery is a direct cloud data warehouse rival, paired with Gemini AI.

competitors.name: Oracle
competitors.note: Oracle Database and Autonomous Data Warehouse for large enterprises.

competitors.name: Teradata
competitors.note: Legacy enterprise data warehouse vendor whose customers Snowflake often wins.

competitors.name: SAP
competitors.note: SAP Business Data Cloud and Datasphere for analytics on SAP business data (also a Snowflake partner).

competitors.name: MongoDB
competitors.note: Operational databases for apps, overlapping with Snowflake's new Postgres and Unistore transactional push.

competitors.name: Datadog
competitors.note: Observability, now a Snowflake market after the February 2026 Observe acquisition.

competitors.name: Palantir Technologies
competitors.note: Foundry and AIP data integration and AI agents for enterprises (also partners with Snowflake).

competitors.name: IBM
competitors.note: watsonx.data lakehouse and Db2 data tools.

competitors.name: Salesforce
competitors.note: Data Cloud and Informatica data management compete for customer-data use cases.

competitors.name: Cloudera
competitors.note: Private hybrid data platform for on-premises and cloud data lakes.

threats: Databricks growing about 80% a year to a revenue run-rate above $7 billion (August 2026) and winning AI and data-engineering workloads
Hyperscalers (AWS, Microsoft Fabric, Google BigQuery) bundling cheaper native data services while also being Snowflake's infrastructure suppliers
Open table formats such as Apache Iceberg making data easier to move and query with other engines
Consumption pricing that lets customers cut usage quickly in a downturn or through optimisation
Rising AI compute costs pushing non-GAAP product gross margin guidance down to 74% for FY2027 from 76%
Security incidents, such as the 2024 data-theft campaign against customer accounts that lacked multi-factor authentication, and resulting litigation
Continued GAAP losses and heavy stock-based compensation ($1.71 billion in FY2026)

ceo.name: Sridhar Ramaswamy
ceo.background: Computer scientist (BTech IIT Madras; MS and PhD in computer science, Brown University); former Google SVP of ads and commerce, co-founder of search engine Neeva, which Snowflake bought in 2023

c1.evidence: Snowflake is one of the two leading independent cloud data platforms in a fast-growing market (product revenue up 37% in Q2 FY2027), but it shares leadership with Databricks and the hyperscalers.

c2.evidence: Customers choose it for a fully managed, easy multi-cloud platform and live data sharing (126% net revenue retention), but Databricks, Microsoft Fabric and Google BigQuery offer close substitutes, so the edge is not clearly lasting.

c3.evidence: Snowflake is well known among IT and data teams (829 Forbes Global 2000 customers) but most ordinary people do not recognise it, and it is not the undisputed default the way Google is in search.

c4.evidence: Its mission to empower every enterprise to achieve its full potential through data and AI is repeated in hiring and AI messaging, but it is a business-efficiency mission rather than a cause ordinary people would feel.

c6.evidence: “data cloud, expensive, AI, fast-growing”: among business and tech audiences the impression is mostly positive about the product, tempered by worries about its cost and its high stock valuation.

c7.evidence: Snowflake estimates its addressable market will grow from $225 billion in FY2026 to $460 billion in FY2031, driven by cloud data and AI agents.

c8.evidence: It has expanded from data warehousing into AI agents (CoWork, Cortex Code), Postgres transactional databases (Crunchy Data, 2025) and observability (Observe, February 2026).

m1.evidence: Ramaswamy has set out a clear view that “the agentic enterprise runs on Snowflake”, calling AI a once-in-a-lifetime technology shift, and has pushed products toward AI agents.

m2.evidence: He is not a founder (CEO since February 2024) but did found Neeva and leads with a long-term product and AI focus; the co-founders are no longer running the company.

m4.evidence: There is little independent evidence either way on whether Ramaswamy leads in a servant style toward employees and customers.

m5.evidence: Under Ramaswamy Snowflake has shipped products faster (Snowflake Intelligence/CoWork, Cortex Code, Openflow, Snowflake Postgres), but its culture was largely shaped earlier by Frank Slootman's intense execution style.

m6.evidence: Ramaswamy holds a PhD in computer science from Brown and was a database researcher at Bell Labs before engineering roles at Google, and he talks in detail about the product.

m7.evidence: He founded Neeva as an ad-free, privacy-focused search engine, which suggests values beyond profit, but there is little other public evidence of his broader stewardship.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Ramaswamy at a top university was found in the sources checked.

m8b.evidence: Ramaswamy is a low-key, technical leader rather than a widely known public personality.

m9.evidence: Since he took over in February 2024, product revenue growth accelerated from about 30% in FY2025 and FY2026 to 37% in Q2 FY2027, and FY2027 guidance was raised to $6.07 billion.

m10.evidence: Snowflake is not known for frugality: it paid $1.71 billion in stock-based compensation in FY2026 and spends heavily on sales and marketing.

c10.evidence: Its platform helps thousands of companies run analytics and AI behind services many people use, but the benefit to ordinary people is indirect.

p2.evidence: Running a secure, elastic, multi-cloud data platform at its scale is technically hard, but several large rivals have built comparable services.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose every year, from $592.0 million in FY2021 to $4,683.9 million in FY2026.

f2.evidence: GAAP gross margin rose from 62.4% in FY2022 to 67.2% in FY2026 and operating margin improved from -58.6% to -30.6%, though the operating margin dipped in FY2025 (-40.2% vs -39.0%).

f3.evidence: At July 31, 2026 it held $4.33 billion of cash and investments against $2.28 billion of convertible notes, with $1.22 billion of FY2026 operating cash flow and $2.15 billion of positive equity.

f4.evidence: Operating cash flow rose every year from $110.2 million in FY2022 to $1,221.9 million in FY2026, but GAAP operating losses widened from $715.0 million to $1,435.2 million.

v1.evidence: Snowflake is known as the easiest fully managed data platform to use, but Databricks is seen as at least as strong for AI and data science, so it is not clearly the best for every buyer.

v2.evidence: No recent top-tier employer ranking for Snowflake was confirmed in the sources checked, though it pays heavily in stock to attract engineers.

c5.evidence: If Snowflake disappeared, data teams at thousands of companies, including 829 of the Forbes Global 2000, would lose their analytics and AI systems for a time, but rivals could eventually replace it.
